title: The Fitrah That Never Died • On the Road to Syria • The Hand That Was Kept From Blood • Al-Amin • Can I Be Trusted? • Khadijah (RA) • The One Zayd Would Not Leave • The Ruling on the Black Stone • A Ruling in Which No One Loses • The Cave of Hira • The Last Word

blocks.1: One thing was becoming clear at this age already. All around, everyone was bowing before idols; he was not. Everyone was eating the meat of animals slaughtered in the name of idols; he would not touch it.{{1}}
blocks.2: No one taught him. No Book had yet come down. It was the fitrah within him that held him back.
blocks.3: The matter is this. The Quraysh did not go to ‘Arafat at Hajj time; they stopped at Muzdalifah. Their reasoning was, we are the residents of the Haram; why should we go outside the Haram! But Ibrahim’s (AS) rule was to stand at ‘Arafat. Jubayr ibn Mut‘im says, once I went to ‘Arafat to look for my lost camel and saw Muhammad standing there. And he is a man of the Quraysh!{{1}}
blocks.4: A whole tribe is following a wrong rule. And one young man, telling no one, held on to the right rule.
blocks.5: There is one more incident in sound hadith; an example of how he was guarded from Jahili habits besides idol worship. As a boy he was carrying stones for the repair of the Ka‘bah. His uncle said, take off your izar and put it on your shoulder, it will ease the chafing of the stones. The moment he took it off he fell unconscious. After that, never in his whole life did anyone see him naked.{{1}}
blocks.6: He did not yet know that he would be a prophet. But Allah never let his fitrah go out.
blocks.7: That fitrah is inside us even today.
blocks.8: The pang inside before telling a lie, that is the fitrah.
blocks.9: The unease when taking unlawful money in hand, that too.
blocks.10: When it is answered the first time, it speaks loudly.
blocks.11: Pressed down again and again, in time it speaks no more.
blocks.12: It does not go out; we ourselves put it out.
blocks.14: The Prophet {{1}} was then twelve. His uncle Abu Talib was setting out on a trading journey to Syria. The nephew would not be left behind at any cost; in the end the uncle took him along.
blocks.15: On the road to Syria, the town of Busra. At the edge of the town an old stone church. Inside lived a monk. His name was Buhayra. How long he had been there, no one knew. The one before him had left this church and an old book. In the book were written the signs of the last prophet; what he would look like, where he would come, what mark would be on his body. Buhayra had read those few lines so often that they were by heart.
blocks.16: Every morning he would come and stand at the door. Over the desert caravans went, caravans came. Rows of camels, clouds of dust, a crowd of weary faces. He searched for one face. In the evening he would shut the door and go inside. The next day again. In this way his hair had turned white, his back had bent. The face he never found.
blocks.17: That day a caravan from Makkah came and halted near Busra. This caravan had passed this way before. Buhayra had never even glanced at it. But today he left the door and came out. His eyes caught on a patch of the sky. Sunlight over the caravan. Only at one spot, a piece of cloud, moving along giving shade. When the caravan halted, the cloud halted too.
blocks.18: Buhayra sent men and invited the whole caravan to eat. He said, come, all of you. Old, young, small, great, slave, free; let none be left out. All came. One by one he looked at the faces. Not there. The face he was looking for was not there. He said, has anyone stayed behind among you? They said, only a boy. The youngest of all. We left him guarding the camels. Buhayra said, call him.
blocks.19: The boy came. A twelve-year-old orphan, sunburned, covered in dust. Buhayra went on looking. Eyes, face, hands, manner of walking. Every line of the book seemed to be walking before him. He asked a few questions; about sleep, about being alone. The answers matched. Then he said gently, child, will you show me your back? The cloak was moved aside. Between the two shoulders, that mark. Exactly where it ought to be, exactly as it ought to be.
blocks.20: Buhayra’s voice shook. The waiting of his whole life stood before him; in the form of a boy. But he knew he could not keep this boy. He took the uncle Abu Talib’s hand. He said, who is this boy to you? Abu Talib said, my son. Buhayra shook his head. He said, no. This boy’s father is not meant to be alive. Abu Talib said, you are right. He is my brother’s son. His father died while he was still in his mother’s womb. Buhayra said, you have spoken truly. Now listen to me. Take him back to his country. Keep him safe from the eyes of the Jews. If they see him, and learn what I know; they will try to finish him. Something great awaits this nephew.{{1}}
blocks.21: The caravan took the road again. Buhayra stood at the door. The cloud of dust grew smaller and smaller and vanished. The face for whose waiting he had spent his whole life, that face appeared once and went. He knew he would not see it a second time.
blocks.22: One thing needs saying here. This incident is very famous in the Seerah books. But there is weakness in its chain; the detailed conversation is not the main evidence. So when telling it in gatherings it is safest to say this much. And the main point is only this: even sitting in the darkness, some of the People of the Book were matching the signs and waiting for that light.
blocks.23: About another side of the journey, however, there is no doubt. A boy of twelve crossed the desert for several months. He saw a different country, a different language, a different religion. He saw Roman rule, the church’s priests, the trade of the markets. The man who would one day carry the call to the whole world saw the world with his own eyes in childhood.
blocks.24: The uncle, had he wished, could have left the boy at home.
blocks.25: The road was long, the sun harsh, the dangers not few.
blocks.26: He did not leave him; he took him along.
blocks.27: We seat our children at the study table.
blocks.28: The outside world he knows through the mobile phone.
blocks.29: How people buy and sell, how they speak, how they are cheated; he sees none of it.
blocks.30: The boy who never went to the market with his father, how will he handle the market when he grows up!
blocks.31: The Hand That Was Kept From Blood
blocks.32: At the age of fifteen or sixteen Harb al-Fijar broke out in Arabia. The Arabs held four months of the year as sacred months. In these months bloodshed was forbidden. This was their only dam. That very dam they broke; they started a war in the sacred months. So the war itself got the name Fijar; that is, transgression.{{1}}
blocks.33: In one corner of that field he too was present. He had come with his uncles. He held no sword. No bow. He only picked up from the ground the arrows the enemy had shot and handed them to his uncles. He himself said later that on that day he did not shoot even a single arrow at anyone. The hand with which one day the bloodshed of all Arabia would be stopped, that hand too was kept from blood even that day.
blocks.34: Some time after this war an incident took place in Makkah. A merchant of the Zubayd tribe of Yemen had come with goods. ‘As ibn Wa’il bought the goods; an influential leader of Makkah. He bought them indeed, but did not pay the price. The man went to the leaders of the Quraysh one by one. Everyone turned away. Because he was an outsider; there was no tribe behind him.
blocks.35: At last he climbed to the top of Mount Abu Qubays and began to recite verses at the top of his voice. O descendants of Fihr! In the heart of Makkah an oppressed man has been wronged! That cry struck the conscience of the Quraysh. Several tribes gathered in the house of ‘Abdullah ibn Jud‘an. There they pledged; if any oppressed person in Makkah is wronged, we will all stand beside him together. Whether he is of Makkah or an outsider. The name of this pact is Hilf al-Fudul.{{1}}
blocks.36: In that gathering the young Muhammad {{1}} was also present. Many years after prophethood he said, in the house of ‘Abdullah ibn Jud‘an I was part of a pact for which, even if I were given red camels, I would not be pleased in exchange; and even in the time of Islam if I were called to it, I would respond. The pact was made in the Jahili age, with polytheists. Still, even after Islam came he supported it. Because justice is justice; whoever does it.
blocks.38: First we see who committed the wrong. Then we decide whether it is a wrong.
blocks.39: If it is one of our own party, we look for explanations.
blocks.40: If it is another party’s, we raise our voices.
blocks.41: To which party the oppressed man belongs, the Prophet {{1}} did not ask that question.
blocks.42: He only saw that the man was oppressed.
blocks.44: In youth he entered trade. And trade is exactly the place where a person’s inside comes out first.
blocks.45: Since childhood the people of Makkah had been noticing that this boy was different. He keeps his word. He does not lie, not even in jest. When he gets someone’s thing in hand he returns it exactly. So gradually, instead of calling him by his real name, they began to call him al-Amin; the trustworthy. No party gave the name, no announcement set it going. It had settled by itself on people’s lips.
blocks.46: There one can give short measure. Put the bad goods at the bottom and arrange the good on top. Sell hiding the defect. And no one will even know.
blocks.47: He did none of these. So the people of Makkah gave him a new name. Al-Amin. And along with it another name; al-Sadiq, the truthful.
blocks.48: The weight of the name can be understood from one incident. After prophethood one day he climbed Mount Safa and called the Quraysh. When all had gathered he said, if I tell you that behind this mountain an army is coming to attack you; will you believe me? They all said at once, yes. We have never heard you tell a lie.{{1}}
blocks.49: An incident before prophethood. He had made a sale with a man named ‘Abdullah ibn Abi al-Hamsa’. Some payment remained due. ‘Abdullah said, you stand right here, I will bring the money. Then he went home and completely forgot the matter. After three days he remembered. Running back he found the Prophet {{1}} still standing in that same place. He only said, you have put me to hardship. For three days I have been here waiting for you.{{2}}
blocks.50: How deep this trust was can be understood from one thing. On the night of the Hijrah the enemies surrounded his house with swords in hand. Even that night he was leaving ‘Ali (RA) behind; to return the trusts that people had deposited. Those who had come to kill him, their trusts too were kept in that very house.{{1}}
blocks.51: This is being said by those who from the very next moment will begin opposing him. Who will stone him, boycott him, plot to kill him. Even they admit, this man never told a lie. This testimony from the mouth of the enemy is the greatest human proof of prophethood.
blocks.53: The name was given by the people of Makkah themselves. There was no announcement. No party proclaimed it. It had settled on people’s lips.
blocks.54: Now ask yourself a question. By what name do the people of my area know me? The answer is not in my hands. I do not give the name; people give it. And people give it seeing my conduct.
blocks.55: There is a simple test. Suppose you are suddenly going somewhere. With whom will you leave the key of your house? The one whose name comes to mind, he is the al-Amin of his area. Now ask the reverse question. Whose mind will my name come to?
blocks.56: And here is the real point. When the Prophet {{1}} stood on Mount Safa and asked, will you believe me; the whole Quraysh said at once, yes. Yet from the very next moment they were his enemies. The enmity came over the message; not over the man. They could not call forty years of character a lie.
blocks.57: Now to today. We speak of da‘wah, we speak of advice. But if the person I am speaking to knows that I give short measure, my words will not enter his ear. Because before listening, people look at the speaker.
blocks.58: One thing is worth noticing. For forty years before prophethood he gave not one invitation. He only lived. And that living itself had become his greatest invitation. Because the day he first spoke, his character had been bearing witness for forty years.
blocks.59: Begin one thing from today. This week keep such honesty in one transaction that at least one person says in his heart; this man can be trusted. One is enough. The name spreads from there.
blocks.61: In Makkah there was a noble businesswoman. Her name was Khadijah bint Khuwaylid. She employed men and sent goods to Syria. Hearing of al-Amin’s good name she sent a caravan with him.
blocks.62: The caravan returned. The profit was more than other times. And the employee Maysarah, returning, gave an account that made Khadijah (RA) stop. Not the account of money. The conduct of the man.
blocks.63: Then she herself sent a proposal of marriage. She was then forty. And he twenty-five.{{1}}
blocks.64: She was one of the noblest women of Makkah. Many proposals had come to her. She had turned them all down. And she chose an orphan young man, in whose hands was no wealth. Because what she was looking for was not wealth. It was character.
blocks.65: This marriage lasted twenty-five years. In these twenty-five years he took no other marriage. One thing is worth noticing here. For those who raise objections about the Prophet’s {{1}} multiple marriages, these twenty-five years are the greatest answer. In the full bloom of youth, at twenty-five, he married a forty-year-old widow; and in her lifetime brought no one else into the house. One who wished to take the path of indulgence would not begin life this way. And even after Khadijah’s (RA) death he remembered her all his life.
blocks.66: ‘A’ishah (RA) says, I was never as jealous of any of the wives of the Prophet {{1}} as I was of Khadijah; though I had never even seen her.{{2}}
blocks.67: Because when a goat was slaughtered in the house he would send meat to Khadijah’s friends too. One whose friends are looked after even after death, how much must she have been loved!
blocks.68: How is our relationship with our wife’s relatives!
blocks.69: The one who stays at home and carries the whole household along, when her father’s family comes, what is the look on our faces!
blocks.70: The Prophet {{1}} did not forget his wife’s friends even many years after her death.
blocks.71: And we forget her people even while the wife is alive.
blocks.72: The One Zayd Would Not Leave
blocks.73: In Khadijah’s (RA) house there was a boy. His name was Zayd ibn Harithah. As a child, in a raid, he had been seized and sold in the market of Makkah as a slave. Khadijah had bought him; later after the marriage she gave him as a gift to the Prophet {{1}}.
blocks.74: Meanwhile Zayd’s father, having lost his son, was nearly mad. Year after year he had searched. At last he got news that his son was in Makkah, in Muhammad’s house. He came to Makkah with the ransom money, bringing Zayd’s uncle along. Standing before the Prophet {{1}} he said, give my son back; take whatever sum you need.
blocks.75: The Prophet {{1}} said, let me call him. If he chooses you, take him without any money. And if he chooses me, I will not hold anyone by force. Zayd was called. His father said, do you know me? He said, yes. This is my father, this is my uncle. The Prophet {{2}} said, you know how I am with you. Now choose; will you go with them, or stay with me?
blocks.76: Zayd did not delay a moment. He said, I want no one more than you. You are my father, you are my everything. The father said in astonishment, you choose slavery, leaving freedom? Zayd said nothing. He knew, staying in this house is not slavery.{{1}}
blocks.77: That very day the Prophet {{1}} took him to the Hatim and declared, be witnesses; Zayd is my son; he is my heir, I am his heir. After that people called him Zayd ibn Muhammad; Zayd the son of Muhammad. Many years later the Qur’an came and gave back the real name; Zayd ibn Harithah.
blocks.78: A father’s affection standing before him. Freedom in the grasp of his hand. Yet a boy gave all that up and chose the company of one man. Why? Because he had seen in this man something that overcomes even the pull of blood. The name of this seeing is love.
blocks.79: The boy who works in the house, the employee who sits in the shop, will he want to stay!
blocks.80: Or will he go elsewhere as soon as the pay rises a little!
blocks.81: That day before Zayd stood his own father, stood his own country, stood freedom.
blocks.83: People can be held in this way; one only has to be a person worth holding on to.
blocks.84: The Ruling on the Black Stone
blocks.85: He was then thirty-five. The House of the Ka‘bah had fallen into disrepair. In a flood the wall had cracked. The Quraysh decided, the House would be rebuilt. And rebuilt only with lawful wealth; money from usury, money from gambling or money from oppression would not be used in this work. A people that worshipped idols; yet in the matter of Allah’s House they had this much sense.
blocks.86: The work was divided. One wall to each tribe. All was going well. Then came the turn of placing the Black Stone.
blocks.87: Now came the trouble. Who would place that stone! Every tribe said, this honour is ours. Words grew. Then swords came out. One tribe dipped their hands in a bowl of blood and took an oath; we will die, but we will not give it up. For four or five days Makkah stood on the brink of war.
blocks.88: At last an old man proposed. Whoever enters the Haram first tomorrow morning, he shall decide. All agreed. Next morning, seeing the one who came in through the door, everyone cried out together— Al-Amin! We accept his ruling.
blocks.89: He asked for a cloth. He spread the cloth on the ground and with his own hands put the stone in the middle of it. Then he said, let each tribe hold one end of the cloth. Lift it together. The cloth rose. Everyone’s hand shared in that honour. Then with his own hands he lifted the stone and set it in its place.{{1}}
blocks.90: The dispute that for four or five days had been heading toward war ended on one cloth. No one lost. Everyone won. And the one who gave the ruling was not yet a prophet. Only thirty-five. Even so all of Makkah put down its swords at a single word of his. Because they knew this man would take no one’s side.
blocks.91: A Ruling in Which No One Loses
blocks.92: For four or five days Makkah stood on the brink of war. Swords drawn. Hands dipped in bowls of blood for the oath. And all of it over who would lift one stone.
blocks.93: Our quarrels are just like this. Who gets the chair of the mosque committee. Who leads the funeral prayer. Whose name is said first in the milad gathering. Who sits down to eat first at the wedding.
blocks.94: The quarrel’s size is small. But the thing inside is one; the share of honour. And a quarrel over a share of honour lasts longest. Because money can be divided; honour cannot be divided.
blocks.95: He did exactly that. He spread the cloth. Every tribe held one end. The honour was shared.
blocks.96: What did he not do! He did not say, you are all wrong. He blamed no one. He did not say to any side, step aside. He found a way in which no one’s name went down.
blocks.97: Why do our settlements break down? Because we sit to decide with the thought, who is right and who is wrong. If you prove one man wrong, he will accept, but he will not forget. And one who does not forget looks for his chance.
blocks.98: And how old was he then! Thirty-five. Prophethood had not yet come. No power in his hand, no army behind him. Even so four tribes accepted his word without question. Because no one had any doubt about his impartiality.
blocks.99: Take up one task at the end. Two people you know have stopped speaking. Do not go about finding out who is right. Look for a way in which neither of the two has to bow his head. Spread the cloth.
blocks.101: As the years grew, a restlessness grew too. Nothing he saw around him satisfied his heart. People bowing before stones. Girl children being buried in the ground. The strong lording over the weak. And no one has any answer to this.
blocks.102: Then he began to stay alone. A little way from Makkah, Jabal al-Nur. Near its peak a small cave; Hira. Taking food for a few days he would go there. When the food ran out he would return, take more, and go again.{{1}}
blocks.103: What did he do there? The word in the hadith is tahannuth. That is, worship and meditation. No fixed rule had yet been revealed. No prayer, no fasting, no Book. Even so he was searching.
blocks.104: And even before this, one thing had begun. True dreams. ‘A’ishah (RA) says, the revelation began with true dreams. Whatever dream he saw, it came out clear before him like the light of dawn.
blocks.105: Prophethood did not come suddenly. For forty years the preparation was going on. His chest was washed. Patience was taught through tending sheep. His trustworthiness was tested in trade. The pain of the orphan was made known to him. He was seated in a pact of justice. And at last he was made alone. In a cave.
blocks.106: Before prophethood Allah taught him to love solitude.
blocks.107: And we cannot be alone for a single moment.
blocks.108: Getting into a lift, the phone. At the dining table, the phone. Before sleep, the phone.
blocks.109: The very habit of sitting quietly has gone.
blocks.110: The person who cannot sit with himself, when will he sit with Allah!
blocks.111: In that very cave one day someone would come and say, read. And with that one word the history of the world would be split in two. That story is in the next lesson.
blocks.113: At the beginning I said, everyone was waiting for him. The People of the Book knew he was coming. The monks sat matching the signs. Zayd, Waraqah, Salman; were wandering in search of the truth.
blocks.114: And he for whom this waiting was, himself? He did not even know that he would be a prophet. But for forty years he was being prepared. The heart was readied, patience was taught, trustworthiness was tested, hardship was made known to him, and he was seated in the gathering of justice. And his character was kept so flawless that even the enemy called him al-Amin. Now the word for us.
blocks.115: We speak of da‘wah, we speak of the religion. But the man who has been cheated by me in the shop, will he listen to me! The neighbour who knows I do not keep my word, will he accept my call! Before da‘wah, character. This order he showed with his own life; forty years of character, then twenty-three years of da‘wah.
blocks.116: That forty years of preparation ended in a cave. There one day someone came and said, read. And with that one word the history of the world was split in two. That story is in the next lesson.

117.title: Practical Resolve
117.text: The child who had no father, whose mother left, whose grandfather did not remain either; Allah raised him with His own hand.

blocks.118: Today I will ask myself one question: is there a child like this around me, who has no one?
blocks.119: Today I will find out his name, and call him by name once, which from today on I will not give up.

footnotes.0: Musnad Ahmad; the report of Zayd ibn Harithah (RA) and Ibn Ishaq. The Prophet {{1}} never worshipped an idol even before prophethood and never ate anything slaughtered in the name of an idol.
footnotes.1: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 1664; on the authority of Jubayr ibn Mut‘im (RA). He says, going to look for one of my camels I saw the Prophet {{1}} standing at ‘Arafat; though he was a man of the Quraysh.
footnotes.2: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 364; Sahih Muslim, hadith 340; on the authority of Jabir (RA). On the Prophet’s {{1}} losing consciousness on removing the izar at the time of the Ka‘bah’s repair, and never afterwards being seen naked.
footnotes.3: The account of Buhayra the monk is in Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi, hadith 3620; on the authority of Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari (RA). The report is famous; but many scholars of hadith have given the opinion that some parts, including the mention of the presence of Abu Bakr and Bilal (RA), have objections of time and chain. The main point — the knowledge of signs among the scholars of the People of the Book — is supported in the Seerah and tafsir.
footnotes.4: Sirah of Ibn Hisham, 1/184–187; on Harb al-Fijar.
footnotes.5: Sirah of Ibn Hisham, 1/133–135; Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah; on Hilf al-Fudul.
footnotes.6: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 4770; Sahih Muslim, hadith 208; on the authority of Ibn ‘Abbas (RA).
footnotes.7: The pre-prophetic dealing with ‘Abdullah ibn Abi al-Hamsa’ (RA) and the three days’ waiting is in Sunan Abi Dawud, hadith 4996. There is a difference of opinion among the scholars of hadith about the chain of the report; but the incident is widely known in the Seerah.
footnotes.8: The purpose of leaving ‘Ali (RA) in Makkah on the night of the Hijrah was to return the trusts people had deposited; see Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah. Those who were plotting the murder had their trusts too in that very house.
footnotes.9: Sirah of Ibn Hisham, 1/187–189; Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra. This reckoning of ages is the well-known account of the Seerah; some reports give a different figure.
footnotes.10: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3816 and 3818; Sahih Muslim, hadith 2435; on the authority of ‘A’ishah (RA).
footnotes.11: Sirah of Ibn Hisham, 1/247–248; on the decision to stay with the Prophet {{1}} rather than go with his father. On being called ‘Zayd ibn Muhammad’ see Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 4782; on the authority of ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar (RA). Later in Surah al-Ahzab, verses 5 and 37, the name ‘Zayd ibn Harithah’ was restored.
footnotes.12: Sirah of Ibn Hisham, 1/192–197; Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah; on the rebuilding of the Ka‘bah and the ruling on the Black Stone.
footnotes.13: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3; Sahih Muslim, hadith 160; the long hadith on the beginning of revelation, on the authority of ‘A’ishah (RA).

quiz.q: Why should the chain be mentioned when telling the story of Buhayra?
o: The story is not very famous in the Seerah books
Fame is no proof, so it is safest to say so
The Christians have objections to the story
Researchers also have doubts about the historicity of the journey
quiz.e: There is no doubt about the other aspects of the journey; the principle learned in Lesson 1 applies here too.

quiz.q: A non-Muslim or non-political platform issued a call to stand by the oppressed. According to the precedent of Hilf al-Fudul, what should be done?
o: To respond only in the case of a Muslim oppressed
To stay completely away
Not to join unless the leadership is in one’s own hands
To respond, because it is a call to justice
quiz.e: The pact was made in the Jahili age with polytheists; yet he said that even in the age of Islam, if called to it, he would respond.

quiz.q: Who were included in the definition of the oppressed in the pledge of Hilf al-Fudul?
o: Everyone, whether of Makkah or from outside
Only people of the Quraysh tribe
Only those with no tribe behind them
Only merchants and people of the caravans
quiz.e: That merchant of Zubayd was an outsider, so no one stood beside him; the pact closed exactly that gap.

quiz.q: What did the Quraysh answer when asked the question standing on Mount Safa?
o: We will think it over and let you know
First show a sign
We believe in the honour of your lineage
We have never heard you tell a lie
quiz.e: Those who from the very next moment would begin opposing him are the ones who gave this testimony.

quiz.q: Someone commits small dishonesties in business and says, no one will even know. What is the direct answer from the lesson?
o: Dishonest trade brings less profit
The one who did none of this was called al-Amin by the people
Giving short measure was forbidden in Arabia
Khadijah (RA) never hired a dishonest employee
quiz.e: Trade is the place where a person’s inside comes out first; and his name the people gave themselves.

quiz.q: What does the lesson call the forty years before prophethood?
o: A silent time of preparation for da‘wah
Only a time of trade and household
A time of no importance
His greatest da‘wah
quiz.e: He gave not one invitation; he only lived. And the day he first spoke, his character had been bearing witness for forty years.

quiz.q: As the way to become ‘al-Amin’ in one’s own area, the task the lesson gives is
o: To keep such honesty in one transaction that at least one person trusts
To arrange to tell people of one’s own honesty
To take up a responsibility in society
Not to be involved in any dealings with anyone
quiz.e: I do not give the name; people give it, and they give it seeing conduct. One is enough; the name spreads from there.

quiz.q: From Khadijah’s (RA) decision in choosing among marriage proposals, which lesson for today’s home does the lesson draw?
o: Difference of age is no barrier
Not wealth, character is the real measure
It is permissible for a woman to send a proposal herself
An employee’s recommendation is important
quiz.e: One of the noblest women of Makkah turned down many proposals and chose a penniless orphan young man.

quiz.q: The expression of the Prophet’s ﷺ love after Khadijah’s (RA) death that the lesson mentions is
o: He used to sit for a long time beside her grave
He used to give charity in her name
He kept her house untouched
He used to send meat to her friends too
quiz.e: One whose friends are looked after even after death, how much must she have been loved!

quiz.q: The condition that the Quraysh themselves set in rebuilding the Ka‘bah was
o: Each tribe would bear an equal share of the cost
The work would begin in a sacred month
Only lawful wealth would be used
No outsider would take part in the work
quiz.e: Money from usury, gambling or oppression would not be used in this work; a people of idol-worshippers, yet they had this much sense.

quiz.q: Why did all of Makkah accept his ruling at only thirty-five, even before he was a prophet?
o: They knew he would take no one’s side
He was the chief of Banu Hashim
He was a wealthy merchant
The whole responsibility for building the Ka‘bah was in his hands
quiz.e: This trust in his impartiality was his greatest capital; and it had been built by the conduct of many years.

quiz.q: By what reason did his ruling in the Black Stone dispute succeed?
o: He was the representative of the largest tribe
By the old man’s proposal everyone was already bound to accept
No one lost, everyone shared in that honour
He was older than everyone in age
quiz.e: Each tribe held one end of the cloth; a four-or-five-day dispute ended on one cloth.

quiz.q: What the Prophet ﷺ did not do in the ruling of the Black Stone was
o: Prove any side wrong
Spread the cloth
Ask all tribes to take part in that honour
Set the stone in place with his own hands
quiz.e: He blamed no one, asked no one to step aside; he found a way in which no one’s name went down.

quiz.q: Why do our settlements break down, what cause does the lesson show?
o: The settler does not have enough power
We sit to work out right and wrong, so one has to lose
Both sides settle their decisions before sitting down
Enough time is not given for the settlement
quiz.e: If you prove one man wrong he will accept but not forget. And one who does not forget looks for his chance.

quiz.q: Two people you know have stopped speaking; from the Black Stone ruling, what should be done?
o: First find out who is right
Call both separately and try to persuade them patiently
Leave it to time
Look for a way in which no one has to bow his head
quiz.e: Spread the cloth; when the honour is shared the dispute ends by itself.

quiz.q: The word that came in the hadith for what he did in Hira is
o: Tahajjud
I‘tikaf
Tafakkur
Tahannuth
quiz.e: That is, worship and meditation; no prayer, fasting or Book had yet been revealed, yet he was searching.

quiz.q: According to ‘A’ishah’s (RA) report, the revelation began with what?
o: Jibril’s (AS) first coming
The habit of retreating in Hira
True dreams
The revelation of Surah al-Muddaththir
quiz.e: Whatever dream he saw, it came out clear before him like the light of dawn.

quiz.q: Among the preparations of the forty years before prophethood, the one the lesson did not mention is
o: The washing of the chest
Testing of trustworthiness in trade
Experience of commanding in war
Tasting the pain of the orphan himself
quiz.e: He was on the field of Fijar, but did not shoot even one arrow; the hand with which bloodshed would be stopped was kept from blood.
